title: A Critical Enquiry of Material Ageing in Interior Architecture
authors: B. Id Saumya Khimesara et al., 2024
research_question: How do material ageing and weathering contribute to the functionality, aesthetics, and value (including sustainability, nostalgia, and historical connection) of interior architecture, particularly in adaptive reuse projects?

participants.description: Architects/designers involved in two adaptive reuse projects (IF.BE and Tianu furniture studio) in Mumbai, India.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Two adaptive reuse projects in Mumbai, India: Tianu (a furniture store in a Victorian building in Ballard Estate) and IF.BE (an old ice factory repurposed as a multifunctional cultural space and café in Ballard Estate). These spaces showcase aged and weathered materials.

measures.construct: Design approach insights for adaptive reuse
Perceived emotional and historical significance of aged materials
measures.instrument: Qualitative analysis of design strategies and outcomes

findings.antecedent: Deliberate removal of brick plaster to expose material imperfections in an old ice factory (IF.BE) during adaptive reuse
findings.consequent: Age (history) is uncovered as a value driver, showing respect for the old
findings.mechanism: Exposing imperfections highlights history and authenticity.
findings.quote: Age (history) as a value driver was Uncovered by deliberately removing the brick plaster and exposing the material's imperfections to pay respect to the old.

findings.antecedent: Minimal new interventions in an old Victorian building adapted for furniture retail (Tianu)
findings.consequent: Sustainability is a key value driver, highlighting the old structure and furniture
findings.mechanism: Minimal intervention respects existing building language, promoting sustainability and highlighting original features.
findings.quote: Sustainability as a key value driver. The new interventions are minimal and not a bold addition. Instead, they follow the language of the existing building.

findings.antecedent: Old buildings, interiors, and architecture (with decay and weathering)
findings.consequent: Evoke nostalgia and historical continuity, drawing people
findings.mechanism: Decay and weathering are charming, emphasizing history and time.
findings.quote: Old buildings evoke nostalgia and historical continuity, which may draw people. Some find these buildings' decay and weathering charming, emphasising their history and time.

findings.antecedent: Old buildings reflecting historical power dynamics (e.g., British colonial heritage)
findings.mechanism: Foucault's theory of power and knowledge suggests cultural objects shape power relations.
findings.quote: Old buildings reflect historical power dynamics, adding to their cultural value.

findings.antecedent: Adaptive reuse of colonial buildings for local use
findings.consequent: May evoke different emotions (pride, connection, discomfort, resentment)
findings.mechanism: Buildings are tangible links to shared history and culture, but colonial legacy has complex associations.
findings.quote: Colonial buildings repurposed for local use may evoke different emotions. These buildings are a tangible link to a shared history and cultural heritage, which may inspire pride and connection. With a colonial legacy still felt today, these buildings may cause discomfort or resentment.

findings.consequent: Can transform negative associations into positive ones, giving a new identity
findings.mechanism: Preserves and modernises the past, revitalising neglected areas.
findings.quote: Adaptive reuse may have given colonial architecture a new identity by transforming negative associations into positive ones.

findings.antecedent: Using original materials and material culture in adaptive reuse
findings.consequent: Preserves the building's authenticity and historical value
findings.quote: Using original materials and material culture in adaptive reuse preserves the building's authenticity and historical value.

findings.antecedent: Juxtaposition of contrasting materials in new interventions during adaptive reuse
findings.consequent: Successful visualisation of new interventions, ensuring historical and contemporary are understood
findings.mechanism: Helps bridge past and present, emphasising historical significance and innovative potential.
findings.quote: juxtaposition* of contrasting materials is often the key to successful visualisation of new interventions, ensuring that the historical and contemporary are understood in their own right and as part of a bigger picture.

mechanisms: Exposing imperfections highlights history and authenticity.
Minimal intervention respects existing building language, promoting sustainability and highlighting original features.
Decay and weathering are charming, emphasizing history and time.
Foucault's theory of power and knowledge suggests cultural objects shape power relations.
Buildings are tangible links to shared history and culture, but colonial legacy has complex associations.
Preserves and modernises the past, revitalising neglected areas.
Helps bridge past and present, emphasising historical significance and innovative potential.
implementation_implications: Designers can better appreciate how to value ageing and weathered materials.
Designers should leverage the enduring value of ageing and weathering materials, promoting sustainability and preserving historical connections in design approaches.
Architects and designers must consider ageing when choosing building materials and designing interiors.
Designers might use decay and time creatively, considering the philosophical aspects of adaptive reuse.
Adaptive reuse preserves old buildings rather than demolishing them, which can destroy their historical, cultural, and architectural value.
Adaptive reuse projects may include structural repairs and upgrades to make the building safe.
Preserving existing resources over new construction makes adaptive reuse a sustainable building design method.
Adaptive reuse requires preserving the history of old buildings.
Interior architecture needs ageing and weathering to add value.
Adaptive reuse repurposes a building to extend its lifespan, add value, and preserve its history and culture.
Reclaiming colonial buildings and using them for local purposes lets communities assert their cultural identity and resist colonial cultural narratives.
The future of colonial buildings will depend on a nuanced and thoughtful approach that balances cultural heritage preservation with colonial legacies.

tables.description: Compares two adaptive reuse projects (IF.BE and Tianu) in Mumbai, India, across categories like location, function, historical significance, old materials reused, reasons for preservation, adaptive reuse approach, innovative solutions, and interview insights.

limitations: Not explicitly stated by the authors.

paper_metadata.title: Recognition Memory for Interior Spaces with Biomorphic or Non–Biomorphic Interior Architectural Elements
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Recognition Memory for Interior Spaces with Biomorphic or Non–Biomorphic Interior Architectural Elements
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: In our study, the primary goal was to gain insights into cognition by measuring spatial memorability for two different types of approaches to geometry in interior design (biomorphic design and non–biomorphic rectilinear design). To better understand the processes behind the memorability differences, we also looked at how spatial memorability interacted with visual attention and spatial pleasantness. After extensive pre–testing, two standardized photographic stimulus sets were created and used during the experiment, controlling for variables such as novelty, complexity, pleasantness, and the number and density of interior architectural elements. Each stimulus set contained equal numbers of photographs with biomorphic elements and photographs with non–biomorphic elements. Subjects ( N = 68 students, mean age = 25.4 years) viewed the first stimulus set, then were given a “distractor” task. Next, subjects viewed the second stimulus set, and for each photograph indicated whether the image was one they had seen or whether it was new. Visual attention for each photograph was monitored using eye–tracking technology, and subjects also rated the pleasantness of each environment. The data were analyzed to test for the relative strength of memorability between environments with biomorphic elements and non–biomorphic elements, as well as the links between recognition memory, visual attention, and pleasantness. The results suggest that interior spaces with biomorphic elements positively contribute to spatial memorability, are found to be more pleasant, and increase visual attention.

environmental_features: aged materials in an old ice factory (IF.BE)

mechanism_chain.description: The deliberate exposure of material imperfections in an old building leads to the perception of its age and history, which in turn drives the attribution of value and respect for the old.

steps.to_construct: uncovering age as a value driver (respect for the old)
